transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE); Priya Menon (Redwood SE); Evan Cole (Thalassa, Head of ML Ops); Maya Lin (Thalassa, CTO); Samir Patel (Thalassa, Quant)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on per-token economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, batching/caching levers, budget constraints and pilot next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood.... Priya and I will run through cost questions and then Priya can take deeper technical perf stuff
[00:12] Evan: Yeah thanks, yeah appreciate it. We're trying to understand if we should go hosted to start or reserve dedicated nodes. Our budget for inference is pretty tight, like focused on sub-$20k mo for initial POC...sorry per month
[00:27] Priya: Got it, and what volumes are you expecting in the POC? qps, token counts, typical prompt/response lengths?
[00:35] Maya: We're looking at 500k tokens/day initially, spikes up to 1.5M on heavy days. Prompts average 120 tokens, responses about 350 tokens. Latency target is 300-400ms tail for user-facing features.
[00:54] Jordan: Ok so that's useful. For hosted we bill per token, and we have a baseline per-1k token rate which varies by model family. For cost-econ discussions it's helpful to think in per-1k active tokens plus amortized overhead for request/response. For example, for a mid-size open model it's around $0.20 per 1k tokens on hosted (ballpark), while Dedicated reserved pricing can drop the per-token unit cost by 30-60% depending on committed throughput and batching.
[01:27] Samir: Wait 0.20 per 1k? That seems a bit high — is that including context or just generation tokens?
[01:33] Jordan: That's total tokens (prompt + completion). And again depends a lot on model size and quantization; smaller quantized variants and 8-bit kernels can push unit costs lower. Also autoscaling and burst affect average.
[01:45] Priya: One lever we often use is batching; continuous batching on the serving runtime can reduce GPU invocations per token. Another is KV/prefix caching — if you have repetitive prompts or shared context across requests we can cache KV to avoid re-encoding. Those two combined can cut per-token billable compute by ~20-40% on typical workloads.
[02:10] Evan: For our workflow we have a lot of repeated system prompts and a large shared knowledge context — sounds like caching could help a lot. How does that work with hosted vs private?
[02:22] Priya: Hosted supports KV cache and prefix caching out of the box, but cache hit fraction depends on how you structure requests. On Dedicated you can pin models and warm the cache proactively, which gives higher effective hit rates and lower tail latency. For Private (VPC) you get full control but you manage the cache warming strategy.
[02:45] Maya: What's the rough tradeoff in committed spend vs unit cost? We're worried about committing if the usage doesn't ramp.
[02:52] Jordan: For Dedicated, we offer reserved capacity with monthly commits; you get much lower per-token when you commit to sustained throughput. If you commit for the POC at say a single GPU pool that covers your 500k tokens/day, the reserved monthly could be in the low thousands, but you need to look at utilization. John's note: (transcription error) — meant Jordan — if utilization is low the effective cost per token rises.
[03:20] Samir: Do you have a model for amortizing the reserved hardware cost into per-token? Like dollars per 1M tokens?
[03:27] Priya: Yes, we typically produce a spreadsheet scenario: take GPU-hour cost, expected throughput for your model (tokens/s), percent batching efficiency, and KV cache hit rate. That yields an effective $/1M tokens. We'll run that for your numbers.
[03:43] Jordan: Important note: quantization and smaller model families can change throughput a lot. In our experience moving from fp16 to 4-bit quantized can increase throughput 1.7x–2x on some kernels, cutting per-token cost similarly, but quality tradeoffs exist.
[04:01] Evan: Hmm quality is important — any eval tooling? You mentioned rollback on regressions.
[04:06] Jordan: Yes Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets and evals; we can hook into your evals and track regressions when switching quantized models.
[04:14] Maya: For compliance we need audit logs and KMS integration if we go private.
[04:18] Priya: Private includes KMS/HSM integration and audit logs, and the Private control plane can be run in your VPC. There's an extra platform fee and enterprise licensing but you keep data residency.
[04:31] Samir: What about burst capacity for spikes to 1.5M? We can't provision for peak daily else it's too expensive.
[04:37] Jordan: We support burst overlays — hybrid routing to hosted fallback or dedicated burst pools. So you can reserve a baseline capacity and fall back to hosted for spikes. Pricing for fallback is standard hosted token rates for overflow.
[04:50] Evan: Ok — so we'd need to understand total expected monthly with some distribution; we can share a 30-day traffic profile.
[04:55] Priya: Perfect, that will let us simulate batching efficiency and effective $/1M tokens.
[05:02] Jordan: A couple of gotchas — network egress can add cost if you run private across regions; also long context windows increase memory and reduce batching efficiency, esp with attention costs. We should look at your typical sequence length distribution.
[05:20] Maya: We'll share prompt length histogram. Also security asked about SOC2 and SSO.
[05:25] Jordan: We have SOC 2 and SAML SSO with RBAC in Console; we'll send SOC2 report and security datasheet.
[05:33] Samir: Any competitors you see customers choosing for cost? We've seen Anthropic and a few infra vendors.
[05:39] Jordan: Some teams use Anthropic or OpenAI APIs for ease but cost can be higher; others self-host with Lambda Labs but then they manage ops. Dedicated gives middle ground: lower unit cost with managed ops.
[05:52] Evan: If you can send a simple model where we plug our 500k tokens/day into your spreadsheet that'd be ideal.
[05:58] Jordan: Yep we'll do that. We'll run two scenarios: hosted only, dedicated baseline + hosted overflow, and private (small VPC) estimate.
[06:07] Priya: For the POC we recommend starting hosted to reduce time-to-value, then switch to a dedicated pool if you hit sustained throughput beyond the break-even. We'll calculate the break-even point in the spreadsheet.
[06:20] Maya: Sounds good.
[06:23] Jordan: Alright, last bit — do we want a benchmark? We can run a short latency/cost benchmark on our side if you share sample prompts and qps.
[06:31] Evan: We'll share prompts and expected qps for a typical 1-hour peak, yes.
[06:36] Jordan: Great. Recap of next steps: Jordan send pricing spreadsheet and SOC2/security docs; Priya to run cost simulation; Evan to send prompt set and traffic profile; schedule follow-up next week.
[06:52] Maya: Thanks all
[06:54] Jordan: Thanks everyone, talk soon
